edges.description: Barrier disruption permits direct, contiguous, thrombophlebitic, or bloodstream access to the central nervous system.
Anaerobic organisms that reach CSF persist in an oxygen-poor intracranial focus and amplify the local bacterial stimulus.
Oropharyngeal Fusobacterium seeding can take a septic venous thrombophlebitic route rather than, or in addition to, direct CSF seeding.
Anaerobic growth in the CSF recruits neutrophils and produces acute bacterial meningitis.
Encapsulated Bacteroides fragilis replicating in or next to the meningeal compartment can wall off into an abscess-forming suppurative focus.
Anaerobic bacteria and their cell-wall products in the subarachnoid space are recognized by innate immune receptors, driving the inflammatory signaling cascade.
Meningeal inflammation and raised intracranial pressure alter the level of consciousness.
Neutrophil recruitment into CSF produces a neutrophilic pleocytosis.
Cytokine-driven neutrophil activation generates reactive oxygen and nitrogen species that injure the blood-brain barrier.

edges.description: Septic venous thrombosis and emboli injure central nervous system structures.
Abscess-forming anaerobic virulence can maintain the contiguous purulent focus that complicates anaerobic meningitis.
Focal brain, abscess, or venous injury produces focal neurologic deficits.

nodes.description: Adjunctive corticosteroid given with or before antibiotics to blunt the injurious inflammatory response. The mortality and sequelae benefit is established for acute bacterial (especially pneumococcal) meningitis in general and is extrapolated to anaerobic disease, for which direct evidence is lacking.

evidence.reference_title: Corticosteroids as adjunctive therapy in acute meningitis: a narrative review.
evidence.snippet: Corticosteroids significantly reduce mortality and neurological sequelae in acute bacterial meningitis (particularly pneumococcal), especially when administered before or with antibiotics.

evidence.reference_title: Adjunctive dexamethasone and 30-day all-cause death after hospital admission in paediatric pneumococcal meningitis: a propensity score analysis.
evidence.snippet: After IPTW, the adjusted 30-day death rate was 6% in the dexamethasone group and 12% in the no dexamethasone group (marginal odds ratio 0·39, 95% CI 0·23-0·65).

nodes.description: Metronidazole-containing antimicrobial therapy kills obligate anaerobes in CSF or adjacent abscesses and is paired with broader bactericidal coverage when the organism and susceptibility pattern are not yet known.

evidence.reference_title: Metronidazole therapy of anaerobic bacteremia, meningitis, and brain abscess.
evidence.snippet: In all cases the anaerobic pathogens were eradicated. Five of the six patients recovered.

nodes.description: Meningeal inflammation, brain abscess, ventriculitis, and septic venous thrombosis injure central nervous system tissue and can leave survivors with persistent neurologic deficits.

evidence.reference_title: Anaerobic bacterial meningitis in adults.
evidence.snippet: Despite treatment, 30.8% (4/13) of the patients died. Of the nine survivors, 22.2% (2/9) had a full recovery, while the other 77.8% (7/9) had varying degrees of neurological deficits.

evidence.reference_title: Fusobacterium necrophorum Meningitis 27 Pediatric Cases From a French National Observatory.
evidence.snippet: Twenty children had a "complicated" meningitis, while 7 an "isolated" one. Median age was 4 years old in both groups. In the complicated group, 12 children underwent surgical drainage and 4 died.

nodes.description: Fusobacterium, Bacteroides, Prevotella, Peptostreptococcus/Parvimonas, and Cutibacterium lineages enter CSF or adjacent intracranial foci from ENT, odontogenic, traumatic, postoperative, or device-associated sites.

evidence.reference_title: Anaerobic bacterial meningitis in adults.
evidence.snippet: A total of 14 anaerobic strains were isolated from cerebrospinal fluid specimens, including nine Gram-negative (G(-)) strains: Fusobacterium nucleatum (3), Prevotella species (3) and Bacteroides fragilis (3), and five Gram-positive (G(+)) strains: Propionibacterium acnes (3) and Peptostreptococcus micros (also known as Parvimonas micra) (2)

nodes.description: Strict anaerobes replicate in a purulent meningeal focus and expose local innate immune cells to anaerobic bacterial cell-wall products.

evidence.reference_title: Fusobacterium necrophorum Meningitis 27 Pediatric Cases From a French National Observatory.
evidence.snippet: Fusobacterium necrophorum was isolated in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) by culture (N = 16) or by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (N = 3).

nodes.description: Anaerobic organisms in the cerebrospinal-fluid space provoke a neutrophilic meningeal inflammatory response with CSF pleocytosis, fever, headache, and meningismus.

evidence.reference_title: Meningitis caused by Fusobacterium nucleatum complicated with cavernous sinus thrombosis: A case report.
evidence.snippet: lumbar puncture confirmed neutrophilic meningitis with Fusobacterium nucleatum isolation.

nodes.description: Encapsulated Bacteroides fragilis uses its capsular polysaccharide as an abscess-promoting and antiphagocytic virulence factor that can help sustain purulent anaerobic foci next to the meningeal compartment.

evidence.reference_title: Infection with Bacteroides fragilis: pathogenesis and immunoprophylaxis in an animal model.
evidence.snippet: The abscesses caused by encapsulated strains were shown to be directly attributable to the capsular polysaccharide, which is an important virulence factor of this organism.

nodes.description: Trauma, neurosurgery, implanted CNS hardware, otitis, sinusitis, dental disease, or a local abscess opens a portal through which normally commensal oral, gut, or skin anaerobes can leave their reservoir niche.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical utility of anaerobic culture of cerebrospinal fluid.
evidence.snippet: Anaerobic meningitis is a rare serious clinical condition which mainly affects vulnerable populations and patients with predisposing factors such as head trauma, prior neurosurgical procedures or implantable medical devices such as ventriculoperitoneal shunts or ventricular drains.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical features and prognostic factors in adults with bacterial meningitis.
evidence.snippet: The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness, and a change in mental status was present in only 44 percent of episodes; however, 95 percent had at least two of the four symptoms of headache, fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical features and prognostic factors in adults with bacterial meningitis.
evidence.snippet: On admission, 14 percent of patients were comatose and 33 percent had focal neurologic abnormalities.

evidence.reference_title: [Clinical observation of 8 cases with central nervous system anaerobic infection diagnosed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing of cerebrospinal fluid].
evidence.snippet: Among the 8 patients, 7 cases had headache and fever as the first symptoms, and 1 case had left-sided limb weakness as the first symptom.

nodes.description: Activated neutrophils release superoxide and nitric oxide, forming peroxynitrite; the resulting oxidative stress drives lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial damage, and blood-brain barrier breakdown. Also extrapolated from pneumococcal meningitis rather than measured in anaerobic disease.
nodes.id: Oxidative Stress and Blood-Brain Barrier Breakdown

evidence.reference_title: Pathophysiology of acute meningitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and adjunctive therapy approaches.
evidence.snippet: polymorphonuclear are attracted, activated and released in large amounts of superoxide anion and nitric oxide, leading to the peroxynitrite formation, generating oxidative stress. This cascade leads to lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial damage, blood-brain barrier breakdown contributing to cell injury during pneumococcal meningitis.

nodes.description: Oropharyngeal Fusobacterium can extend to septic internal jugular or cavernous sinus venous thrombophlebitis (Lemierre physiology), a contiguous venous route to intracranial injury recognized in anaerobic meningitis.

evidence.reference_title: Meningitis caused by Fusobacterium nucleatum complicated with cavernous sinus thrombosis: A case report.
evidence.snippet: Magnetic resonance imaging revealed left cavernous sinus thrombosis requiring anticoagulation.

nodes.description: Surgical excision or drainage of the infected nidus (brain abscess, subdural empyema, infected device, or parameningeal focus) removes the anaerobic source that seeds and sustains the meningeal infection, and is paired with prolonged anaerobe-active antibiotics.

evidence.reference_title: Microbiology and treatment of brain abscess.
evidence.snippet: Once an abscess has formed, surgical excision or drainage combined with prolonged antibiotics (usually 4-8weeks) remains the treatment of choice.

nodes.description: Bacterial recognition by Toll-like receptors on antigen-presenting cells activates NF-kappaB and MAPK pathways, upregulating cytokines and chemokines that recruit and activate neutrophils in the subarachnoid space. This step is extrapolated from pneumococcal meningitis models rather than measured in anaerobe-induced disease.

evidence.reference_title: Pathophysiology of acute meningitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and adjunctive therapy approaches.
evidence.snippet: S. pneumoniae is recognized by antigen-presenting cells through the binding of Toll-like receptors inducing the activation of factor nuclear kappa B or mitogen-activated protein kinase pathways
